title: Ecosystem code defaults to Apache 2.0 while trademarks are held by Foundations under governance instruction
content:
A.2.9.1.9 sets two asymmetric policies. Code and assets "should generally" be released under Apache 2.0 "unless there are specific and clear reasons to use a different license, as determined by the Core Facilitator" — permissive by default, with copying, modification, and commercial reuse allowed. Simultaneously, the Core Facilitator "must ensure that a Foundation and other appropriate legal entities exists to properly protect intellectual property and trademarks," all actors "must take steps to protect the brands and trademarks," and such entities "must over time be set up to follow instructions from Sky Governance."

The split is deliberate and well-chosen. Giving away the code maximizes adoption, forkability, and credibility as public-good infrastructure — and Apache 2.0 specifically carries a patent grant, which matters in a domain where patent trolling appears explicitly in the Lawyer Registry's covered areas.

The brand is the retained asset. Anyone may run the code; only Sky may call the result Sky. That is the standard open-source moat, and it locates the enforceable exclusivity in trademark rather than copyright, which is far cheaper to defend and does not compromise the openness claim.

The structural loose end is the phrase "over time." Foundations hold the trademarks now and are only progressively being wired to follow governance instruction, so the ecosystem's one exclusive asset currently sits with entities whose obedience to SKY holders is aspirational rather than established.
description: Permissive licensing is the default absent clear reasons otherwise as judged by the Core Facilitator, but brands and trademarks are centralized in legal entities that must over time follow Sky
